hero.title: Has he or she slept with someone else?
hero.description: 15 questions to put order into what you have observed. We start by asking who we're talking about, because the questions aren't the same.
hero.subtitle: Free, anonymous, instant result

howTo.title: How does this test work?
howTo.step1: You say whether your partner is a man or a woman. The fifteen questions adapt, and two of them change completely.
howTo.step2: Answer with the last few weeks in mind, not your whole history. A sign counts because it changed, not because it exists.
howTo.step3: Each answer is worth 0 to 3 points. The total places you in one of four levels of reading.
howTo.step4: The result tells you what your observations weigh together, and what it is reasonable to do with them.
howTo.outro: Answer honestly, including when the honest answer is "I don't know". A reassuring result obtained by rounding off the corners is worth nothing.

crossLink.title: Not quite your question?
crossLink.text: If your doubt is more about a friendship that got too close, ambiguous messages or a closeness that makes you uncomfortable, the other test is the one you want.

section1.title: The question that keeps going round
section1.p1: You may not have told anyone. It comes back in the evening, in the car, when the conversation dies down. Have they slept with someone else? And right behind it, a second question, often more painful: am I losing my mind, or am I right?
section1.p2: Doubt has this peculiarity that it feeds itself. A late arrival becomes a lie, a phone turned face down becomes proof, a silence becomes a confession. Then the next day everything looks normal and you blame yourself for having thought it. That back and forth is exhausting, and it damages the relationship just as surely as what you fear.
section1.p3: This test will not decide for you, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. What it does is line up what you have actually observed, separate the signals that carry weight from the ones that carry none, and give you a whole picture instead of fifteen details spinning around in your head.

section2.title: The signs that count, and the ones that prove nothing
section2.intro: None of these signs is worth anything on its own. What counts is the recent change, and the fact that several show up at the same time.
section2.pillar1Text: The signal isn't "they protect their phone", it's "they have been protecting it since recently". New passcode, screen turned over, notifications muted, a conversation archived. Someone who has always been private tells you nothing at all.
section2.pillar2Text: This is the heaviest signal of all, because it can be checked. An evening told twice with two different places, an explanation corrected afterwards. A lie about the place weighs more than a lie about the time.
section2.pillar3Text: In both directions. A sudden stop is a warning, but so is a change of nature: new habits that come out of nowhere raise as many questions as a sudden desert.
section2.pillar4Text: You ask a question, and you end up justifying yourself. When someone accuses their partner of cheating with nothing to suggest it, therapists call that projection. It isn't proof, but it is worth noting.
section2.pillar5Text: A double life is expensive. Unusual cash withdrawals, restaurant or hotel spending invisible in the shared budget, an account opened without a word. Bank statements lie less well than people.
section2.pillar6Text: A pause when you walk in, a friend who avoids you, a half-spoken sentence. Those close by often know first, and they cope badly with knowing. Their discomfort is an indirect signal, and it shows.
section2.tip: Two signs are almost never enough. The word investigators use is "cluster": it is the convergence of several clues over the same period that changes the reading, not their raw number.

section3.title: What your score says, and what it doesn't
section3.p1: The test is scored out of 45. The four levels below are not verdicts, they are ways of reading what you answered. A high score describes a behaviour, never a fact.
section3.row1Analysis: None of the usual signals. If the doubt persists, it probably comes from somewhere other than their behaviour.
section3.row2Analysis: Change, yes. But stress, exhaustion and a phase of withdrawal produce exactly the same symptoms.
section3.row3Analysis: Too many things converge for it to be chance. Careful: depression or a hidden problem gives the same profile.
section3.row4Analysis: Secrecy, verified inconsistencies, withdrawal of intimacy. It still proves nothing, but it calls for an answer.
section3.tip: A score of 40 is not proof, and a score of 8 is not a guarantee. Both mainly tell you what your observation is worth today, with the elements you have.

section4.title: Sleeping elsewhere and getting attached elsewhere are not the same question
section4.p1: Many people arrive here with a precise question: was there a physical act? That is a different question from "is my relationship in danger", and it calls for different signs. Physical infidelity leaves material traces: absences, spending, inconsistencies about places, sometimes a change in intimacy.
section4.p2: Emotional infidelity leaves almost nothing material. It shows in attention that moves elsewhere, in confidences that go somewhere else, in a new closeness with someone who is never mentioned in front of you. It can hurt just as much, and last longer, without a single night spent away.
section4.p3: This test focuses on the first question. If your doubt is more about the second, our infidelity test for couples covers both forms in twenty questions. And if what is eating at you is mostly jealousy, with nothing concrete behind it, the jealousy test fits better.

section5.title: What you really shouldn't do right now
section5.p1: Doubt pushes you to act, and almost every action it inspires makes things worse. Here are the three most common ones.
section5.sub1Text: It's the first idea, and it's the worst. At best you find nothing, and the doubt stays intact because "they must have deleted it". At worst you find something ambiguous that you will never be able to forget or verify. And in both cases, you now have something to hide too.
section5.sub2Text: Questioning their friends puts everyone in an impossible position and always gets back to them, usually distorted. You lose the element of surprise, you gain a reputation, and you get no answer.
section5.sub3Text: "I know you're cheating on me" never produces a confession. It produces a counter-attack, and it puts you in the position of having to prove something. If you accuse with nothing to show, you have lost the discussion before starting it.
section5.tip: If you are tempted by spyware or a tracking device, know that installing that on someone's phone without their consent is a criminal offence in most countries. Beyond the legal risk, it is exactly the kind of act that will cost you the benefit of the truth if it ever comes out.

section6.title: How to ask the question, in practice
section6.p1: There is no magic wording, but there are conditions that clearly raise your chances of getting a real answer rather than a defensive reflex.
section6.sub1Title: Choose the moment, not the impulse
section6.sub1Text: Not at midnight after a night out, not as one of you is leaving for work, not in front of the children. A moment when nobody has an escape route or an appointment in twenty minutes.
section6.sub2Text: "You came home at three on Saturday and told me you were at Tom's, and Tom told me the opposite" is hard to brush aside. "You lie to me all the time" gets brushed aside in one sentence. Stay on the facts you actually observed, without inflating them.
section6.sub3Text: Announcing "I'd rather know, even if it hurts, than carry on like this" often changes the conversation. Many people lie not out of a taste for lying but out of fear of the reaction. Removing part of that fear can be enough.
section6.sub4Title: Listen to what isn't said too
section6.sub4Text: An answer that takes ten seconds to arrive is not proof. An answer that changes version between Tuesday and Thursday is. What you are looking for isn't a reaction, it's consistency over time.

section7.title: And if the answer is yes?
section7.p1: Then you enter another question, and you don't have to answer it that same evening. The first thing to know is that the decision to stay or leave is not taken in the days that follow the revelation. Shock is a poor adviser, in either direction.
section7.p2: What determines the rest comes down to very little: does the person take responsibility without minimising, do they cut contact, do they accept your questions for months without tiring of them. Without those three, rebuilding rarely holds. With them, it is possible, and it generally takes between one and three years.
section7.p3: And if you want to take stock afterwards of what is left, the healthy relationship test and the trust test talk about what comes next rather than about the shock.
section7.tip: If the situation puts you in danger, if you are afraid of your partner's reaction when you ask a question, this is no longer a question of infidelity. A domestic abuse helpline in your country can take that call, free and confidentially.

faq.q1: Can a test really tell whether someone slept with another person?
faq.a1: No, and no serious test will claim it can. What this test measures is the consistency and the density of what you have observed. It turns fifteen scattered impressions into one overall reading. Certainty never comes from a questionnaire: it comes from a conversation, an admission, or something concrete.
faq.q2: Why ask whether my partner is a man or a woman?
faq.a2: Because two of the fifteen questions only make sense for one or the other, and because a question written for a man reads badly when you're thinking of a woman. The choice changes neither the scoring nor the result levels: the other thirteen questions are identical, only the wording follows.
faq.q3: My score is high, does that mean they cheated on me?
faq.a3: No. A high score means a lot of signals piled up over the same period. An undisclosed depression, a hidden dismissal, a debt, a health problem kept secret or an addiction produce exactly the same answer profile. That is why the result points you towards a conversation, not towards a conclusion.
faq.q4: My score is low but I still have a doubt, is that normal?
faq.a4: Yes, and it's common. Doubt doesn't always come from the other person. An old betrayal, in this relationship or a previous one, leaves a vigilance that wakes up without a present-day reason. If the doubt persists while nothing feeds it, that is the side to look at, and talking about it remains the best way out.
faq.q5: Can I take this test with my partner?
faq.a5: It isn't designed for that, and it would be a bad idea: the fifteen questions describe suspicions, and having someone you suspect read them amounts to accusing them one question at a time. Take it alone, then talk, in your own words.
faq.a6: No. Everything happens in your browser, no answer is sent or kept, and there is no account and no email address to give. Close the page and nothing remains.
